reviewDecisions.title: Initial ARDS tidal-volume order
clarityIssues: The task calls this an initial order although a 500-mL breath and plateau measurement have already been delivered. Distinguish selecting the first protective prescription from adjusting an established protective prescription.
PBW is not expanded on first use. Residents will usually recognize it, but 'predicted body weight' is clearer than an unexplained worksheet abbreviation.

cues.phrase: Checked PBW
cues.why: Only one of the three weights receives a validation adjective. Together with 'lung-protective ventilation plan', this gives the worksheet an answer-selecting label rather than requiring an independent interpretation.

cues.phrase: Set tidal volume to 300 mL / Set tidal volume to 450 mL / Set tidal volume to 540 mL
cues.why: All three choices are the same multiplier applied to the three displayed weights. A reader can identify the shared multiplier from the numbers and then select the uniquely 'Checked' weight without knowing the prescription rule.

fairness: 300 mL is the defensible initial 6-mL/kg predicted-weight choice among these options. The explanation appropriately requires subsequent pressure and gas reassessment; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The oxygenation values and elevated plateau do not distinguish these three weight calculations. Removing them leaves the answer unchanged: weight selection plus multiplication is one rule application, not two consequential clinical decisions.
The named age/sex clinic frame is consistent, and the task identifies the historical patient. Initial lung-protective ventilation is a high-yield resident concept.

Review scope: 13 non-held candidate nodes are evaluated in this array. The candidate ards-pressure-limit node carries release hold review.n3.ards-weight-change-versus-tidal-volume-basis.v2 and is excluded, as requested. Historical kept, retired, parked and held records are not adjudicated. This is an offline editorial review, not source re-verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical approval; that limitation applies to every entry.
suggestions: Remove the asymmetric 'Checked' label, expand PBW, and make the temporal wording consistent with the actual order being selected.

Either obtain explicit acceptance for a foundational single-rule item or redesign the options so a clinically meaningful finding changes the chosen plan after the weight calculation. Do not count the multiplication itself as a second consequential step or duplicate the separately held pressure-limit decision.

reviewDecisions.title: Prone positioning after protective ventilation
clarityIssues: 'Which additional respiratory-support intervention' does not accommodate the option to continue the existing intervention. The task should ask for the next respiratory-support plan.

cues.phrase: additional respiratory-support intervention / Continue supine protective ventilation
cues.why: Without medical knowledge, the task rules out the continuation option because it is not an additional intervention. This removes the intended continue-versus-escalate decision before the oxygenation data are interpreted.

fairness: The constructed PaO2/FiO2 ratio is approximately 73, despite adjusted protective support. Proning is the defensible best offered next plan; improved plateau does not resolve the oxygenation problem, and immediate ECMO cannulation is premature without assessment of conventional rescue strategies.
There are two meaningful steps: interpret oxygenation in relation to support, then select the escalation stage. Severe ARDS support sequencing is high yield.

The later entry follows the earlier volume adjustment coherently, repeats the necessary current pressure and oxygenation data, and does not depend on recalling the prior numerical volume. Prior explanations do not teach proning. The intervening held node is not approved by this sequence assessment.
The spine and abdominal observations are relevant to positioning feasibility. They are not themselves nonmedical answer matches and should not be deleted merely to obscure the intended plan.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete task such as 'Which respiratory-support plan should have been chosen next for Nina Cole at this assessment?' Retain continuation as a genuine alternative and recheck the options with the revised task.

reviewDecisions.title: Assessment of a peak-pressure rise

cues.phrase: peak-pressure rise / Measure an end-inspiratory occlusion pressure
cues.why: The key is the only option that explicitly measures a pressure, matching the task's requested problem. The alternatives are anatomical examinations. This is a wording/category advantage even though all three are assessments.

fairness: An inspiratory hold is a defensible first discriminating assessment in this passive, stable, volume-controlled record. There is no clear clinical error in the key or the explanation.

The main demand is recalling which measurement separates resistive from static loading. Stability just permits that assessment; the options do not make a second consequential interpretation necessary. Bronchoscopy is a relatively invasive initial competitor without a supplied airway finding.
Pressure mechanics is high yield. The named patient, historical stage and task are clear, and the later secretion item follows acquisition of the missing pressure coherently.
suggestions: Compare genuinely competing bedside assessments at the same immediate stage, with neutral parallel labels, rather than one pressure measurement against invasive airway and pleural examinations.

For a routine resident item, add a supported acquisition or clinical discrepancy that changes which assessment is appropriate; otherwise seek explicit acceptance as foundational mechanics recognition. Avoid inventing difficulty by withholding the passive/stability conditions.

reviewDecisions.title: Airway intervention after a resistive pressure change

cues.phrase: visible secretions in the endotracheal tube / Preoxygenate and suction the endotracheal tube
cues.why: The only option repeating the named tube removes the plainly visible material. A reader can match this observation to suction without interpreting either pressure.

cues.phrase: Preoxygenate and suction the endotracheal tube
cues.why: The key uniquely bundles a preparatory safety action with treatment; the competing options are single interventions. The preparation belongs in common procedural context or feedback rather than giving only the key a completeness advantage.

fairness: The widened peak-minus-plateau difference with unchanged static pressure supports an increased resistive component, and coarse sounds plus visible secretions make suction the best offered immediate action. Bronchodilation can coexist with secretion management, but this record supports suction priority. No confident clinical error identified.

The pressure comparison can be deleted without changing the answer. The intended mechanics-then-treatment reasoning is therefore bypassable, and prior feedback already prepares the dynamic/static distinction.

The update repeats the prior and current values and relevant ventilator conditions, so the second part is coherent and understandable without remembering earlier measurements. Airway obstruction and ventilator troubleshooting are high yield.
suggestions: Use parallel intervention labels, moving routine preoxygenation instruction to feedback or shared context.

Rebuild the decision around a response to an actual airway-clearance attempt or another supported competing observation so the pressure trend changes the next action. Do not simply delete necessary airway findings while preserving a suction key that would then be underdetermined.

reviewDecisions.title: Ventilator adjustment for incomplete expiration
fairness: The flow label identifies the observation as expiratory, so the negative sign is interpretable without an absent waveform image. Measured total PEEP is clearly distinguished from set PEEP.

The learner must infer incomplete emptying from persisting expiratory flow and the PEEP difference, then resist increasing minute ventilation in response to the rising PaCO2. Reducing rate is the best of these three offered adjustments.

Both distractors are recognizable attempts to improve CO2 clearance and become harmful choices through the supplied mechanical pattern. The directional opposition in the options does not identify the key without physiology knowledge.

The known asthma diagnosis is legitimate context for the different management task. The explanation does not invent a universal permissible pH or rate. No confident clinical inaccuracy or competing equally good listed action identified.
This is a self-contained, high-yield obstructive-ventilation decision; difficulty comes from a real gas-exchange versus emptying tradeoff.

reviewDecisions.title: SBT readiness despite an elevated screening index
clarityIssues: 'A brief unsupported sample' does not establish whether this was merely an index measurement or a breathing trial stopped for intolerance. Duration need not become a new cutoff, but the observed breathing effort, tolerance and reason for ending the sample are decision-critical.
Expand 'rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI)' in the update; its definition currently appears only indirectly in an option.

cues.phrase: A brief unsupported sample reports an RSBI / Repeat the rapid shallow breathing index assessment
cues.why: One distractor repeats the just-completed measurement without any stated acquisition problem. This creates a repeat-versus-new-assessment shortcut and weakens the closest alternative.

fairness: The intended distinction between screening readiness and requiring an RSBI gate is useful and high yield. If the unsupported sample was tolerated and technically interpretable, a monitored SBT is defensible despite the isolated index.

Not requiring calculation of an index does not make a measured adverse respiratory pattern irrelevant. The absent effort/tolerance observations leave uncertainty about whether the index is an isolated screen or evidence of actual trial failure; I am not asserting that 118 itself contraindicates an SBT.

SIMV rate reduction is a weak modern competitor, leaving most discrimination to the underspecified sample-versus-trial distinction. The intended two steps are integrating readiness observations and deciding how much weight to place on the index; ambiguity is not credited as hard difficulty.
The later trial sequence is chronologically coherent, but it does not retrospectively supply the missing tolerance information for this first decision.
suggestions: State the observed effort and tolerance during the short measurement and why it ended. Preserve the elevated index rather than explaining away its interpretation before answering.

Make the nearest alternative a specific, plausible response to the supplied breathing pattern at the same decision stage. Recheck the SBT-versus-defer/reassess ranking with Melissa; do not infer that optional RSBI screening means every high measured index should be ignored.

reviewDecisions.title: Interpreting an SBT performed at increased FiO2
clarityIssues: 'Minimal-support' does not specify the actual pressure support and PEEP used. This matters when an option proposes adding pressure support.
The task asks for a plan 'before an extubation decision' while one option makes that decision.

cues.phrase: before an extubation decision / Extubate to the trial oxygen concentration
cues.why: The task linguistically excludes immediate extubation before the learner evaluates whether the trial supports it.

cues.phrase: charted as tolerated. Sarah remains comfortable, but
cues.why: The adversative wording announces a defect in an apparently successful test. FiO2 is the only changed support variable displayed, and only one repeat option corrects it; the item can be answered as a test-comparison puzzle.

fairness: Reassessment without the increased oxygen support is a defensible best plan among these choices. The explanation appropriately describes conditional, very-low-certainty guidance rather than an absolute extubation prohibition; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The intended interpretation-then-reassessment task is bypassed by the lead-in and weak pressure-support alternative. Recognizing different test conditions is worthwhile, but the current execution is not a difficult two-step resident item.

The before/during oxygen data make the update understandable independently of the prior RSBI answer. Prior feedback does not disclose the FiO2 rule. Valid SBT conditions are high yield, although recall of the exact conditional guideline wording is less valuable than its physiological application.
suggestions: Ask neutrally for the next liberation plan, remove the editorial 'but', and state the actual support conditions needed to compare the offered actions.

Use credible competing plans that require interpreting the oxygenation response, rather than a task-excluded extubation and unsupported pressure escalation. Retain the evidence-certainty limitation in feedback.

reviewDecisions.title: Airway clearance after a tolerated SBT

cues.phrase: Her cough does not move secretions into the endotracheal tube; pooled secretions repeatedly require suction / Continue intubation and airway clearance
cues.why: The update states an immediately unresolved clearance problem, and only the key explicitly addresses clearance. The two extubation options differ in oxygen/support device but neither addresses the dominant problem.

fairness: Continuing intubation while addressing ineffective clearance is the best offered plan. A cuff leak and a tolerated SBT do not establish effective airway clearance. No confident clinical error identified.

This is a single decisive safety finding overriding reassuring results; the normal SBT and cuff leak are not two independent consequential inferences. The current distractors do little to challenge a resident who recognizes the clearance problem.

The repeated trial, alertness and cough observations are present in this update. It follows the preceding trial reassessment coherently and stands alone; prior explanations do not teach the secretion key. The distinction between ventilatory readiness and airway function is high yield.
suggestions: Do not remove the necessary unsafe-clearance observations to manufacture difficulty. Either explicitly seek acceptance as a foundational safety-recognition item or develop a different supported reassessment boundary where actual clearance trajectory changes the extubation plan.
Keep common airway care in shared context and compare parallel concrete airway plans, avoiding a uniquely comprehensive key.

reviewDecisions.title: Initial support for acute-on-chronic COPD ventilatory failure
clarityIssues: The baseline cell under 'PaO2 / oxygen condition' contains only 'Room air', so the table mixes an unreported baseline PaO2 with an actual current value. Mark an unavailable value explicitly or separate the columns.

cues.phrase: an acute COPD exacerbation that initially received mask support / Start bilevel mask ventilation
cues.why: The shared presentation reveals the historical initial support action before the question asks the learner to select it. Only one option is mask support. The gases, work of breathing and airway assessment can all be ignored.

fairness: Without the leak, the acute fall in pH with rising PaCO2, persistent work of breathing and preserved alertness/clearance support bilevel NIV over oxygen alone or immediate intubation. No confident clinical error identified.

The intended two steps are recognizing acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure and assessing suitability for noninvasive support. The presentation supplies the answer, so those steps are not required in the actual item; its current difficulty is easy.

COPD NIV selection is high yield. The named age/sex and initial hospital time point are clear. The later failure and recovery stages are coherent, but the shared presentation should not disclose this first answer.
suggestions: Delete 'that initially received mask support' from the presentation. The initial support can become known in the next update after the learner has answered this node.
Clarify the baseline exhibit cell, then independently re-review the repaired item; the underlying gas-plus-airway reasoning could support a moderate two-step question once the answer leak is removed.

reviewDecisions.title: Escalation during deteriorating NIV
fairness: Invasive ventilation is the single defensible best offered choice given worsening ventilation, markedly reduced responsiveness and pooled secretions. Increasing mask assistance does not resolve the airway-function problem. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The diminished responsiveness and inability to handle secretions already determine the action. The saturation/gas contrast is educational but can be deleted without changing the answer, so the claimed two-step oxygenation-versus-ventilation interpretation is not necessary.

This is an easy high-yield rescue/safety recognition item, not a nonmedical wording giveaway. Necessary danger signs must remain; their clarity should not be treated as an authoring defect to be hidden.

The update states the active support and current trajectory, follows the initial NIV decision coherently, and stands alone without memorizing the previous gases. Prior feedback also prepares the deterioration boundary, further limiting difficulty.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as an intentional safety-recognition exception, or author a different earlier response-assessment decision with credible competing next actions. Do not weaken airway danger signs while preserving this urgent intubation key.

If a moderate/hard item is required, make both the trajectory and a supported NIV-performance observation consequential, with clinician review of the resulting escalation boundary and no invented pH cutoff.

reviewDecisions.title: Planned extubation with preventive NIV
fairness: The learner must recognize return to a compensated chronic baseline rather than demand normal PaCO2, then choose immediate post-extubation support for an older patient with chronic respiratory disease and hypercapnia during the trial. Both observations affect the plan.

Standard oxygen is a credible alternative because low-flow oxygen meets the recorded oxygenation need; preventive ventilatory support requires an additional risk-based inference. Continued intubation represents a recognizable error about chronic PaCO2 rather than an arbitrary absurd option.

Immediate bilevel support is a defensible best choice for this selected profile, and the explanation appropriately avoids ranking all possible HFNC/NIV combinations or extending prophylaxis to every extubation. Offline assessment does not independently verify the exact guideline population or constitute clinical sign-off.

The chronology explicitly advances from invasive support to a tolerated SBT with intact clearance. Current and pre-illness gases are repeated, so the node is interpretable with its shared presentation and update. Prior NIV-failure feedback does not teach the preventive post-extubation decision.

The earlier use of mask support is historical context at this stage, not a reliable answer shortcut: returning to it after a prior failure requires recognizing the changed clinical phase. Preventive versus rescue support and chronic hypercapnia are high-yield distinctions.

reviewDecisions.title: Flow assessment after a falling mixed-venous saturation
clarityIssues: A pulmonary-artery catheter and repeated indirect calorimetry are present, but the record does not state whether cardiac-output measurements are available from that monitoring. This does not make echo wrong, but leaves the claimed clinical priority incompletely motivated.

cues.phrase: Catheter position and sample labels are verified / Repeat the complete blood count / Repeat the arterial blood gas
cues.why: The data have been collected and explicitly validated; both distractors simply repeat represented carriage measurements. Only the key introduces a new assessment. A test-wise reader can select the new investigation without interpreting the direction or magnitude of the venous change.

fairness: At unchanged oxygen consumption, the larger arterial-to-mixed-venous oxygen-content difference supports lower flow. The direction of the inference is internally consistent: hemoglobin rises while the arterial-minus-venous saturation gap also widens. No exact oxygen-content constant or new clinical threshold is required to assess that direction.

Doppler echo can assess output and cardiac contributors, and it is the best offered investigation once the measurements are trusted. That does not establish it is the uniquely prioritized real-world investigation in every pulmonary-artery-catheter setting; this uncertainty is a ranking/context limitation, not a confident clinical inaccuracy.

The underlying physiology could support moderate two-step reasoning, but the only-new-test structure lets the learner bypass it. Deleting the actual numbers still leaves the same test-taking preference.

Oxygen content, extraction and flow are high-yield physiology; ranking echo over redundant repeats has less educational value. The single-node historical clinic record is otherwise understandable and contains a named age/sex patient.
suggestions: Clarify what flow information is actually available and the specific unresolved clinical question, without simply announcing that echo is missing.

Compare equally novel, clinically plausible investigations, or ask a concrete flow-dependent decision whose ranking changes with the paired observations. Preserve sample validity and stable consumption, which are necessary assumptions; do not remove them just to make repeat tests plausible.
Have Melissa resolve the exact investigation priority in the revised context; retain the explanation's refusal to infer a specific shock subtype or treatment from these measurements alone.

reviewDecisions.title: Rescue after established post-extubation deterioration
fairness: The learner must interpret combined worsening oxygenation, ventilation and fatigue despite existing support, then distinguish rescue of established post-extubation failure from preventive NIV. Reintubation is the best offered plan.

Rescue bilevel support is a credible near-miss for an acidotic patient who has not been described as profoundly obtunded; choosing against it requires attention to population and clinical phase. Merely increasing oxygen support does not address the worsening ventilatory trajectory.

The explicit medical, nonoperative and non-COPD context legitimately defines the population rather than naming the key. These findings should not be removed as alleged cues. The explanation preserves conditional guidance and exceptions; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the stated scenario.

This standalone node supplies the preceding extubation, current support, gas trend, work of breathing and unsuccessful initial airway measures. It does not require remembering a separate prophylaxis question. Rescue sequencing is a high-yield critical-care concept.
This is an offline editorial PASS for the exact supplied content, not independent verification of every guideline exception or named-clinician approval.

originalProposedNodes.task: Which initial tidal-volume order best fits Nina Cole’s recorded lung-protective ventilation plan?

choices.label: Set tidal volume to 300 mL
choices.rationale: Six times the checked 50-kg PBW gives 300 mL; the higher current prescription and plateau require protective reassessment.
choices.temptation: Use the lung-size indexing value, not the scale.
choices.correctUnder: The constructed PBW remains 50 kg.

choices.label: Set tidal volume to 450 mL
choices.rationale: This uses 6 mL/kg of the 75-kg pre-illness actual mass, which is not the lung-size basis.
choices.temptation: Mistake a dry actual mass for predicted lung size.
choices.correctUnder: A separately checked PBW of 75 kg with a suitable pressure response.

choices.label: Set tidal volume to 540 mL
choices.rationale: This uses fluid-loaded actual mass and moves away from the protective prescription.
choices.temptation: Treat resuscitation weight as a larger lung.
choices.correctUnder: A separately checked PBW of 90 kg with a suitable pressure response.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: Use the checked PBW for the initial 6-mL/kg order: 6 × 50 = 300 mL. Scale-weight changes do not enlarge the ventilated lung. The delivered volume and plateau must then be reassessed; this calculation does not guarantee the final setting.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Recognize that measured mass and the checked lung-size index are different inputs.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Apply the initial protective target to the correct index and change the recorded order.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Use pre-illness actual mass because it appears less distorted than the current weight.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The independently checked PBW is 50 kg, while both scale measurements are higher.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Using actual mass can deliver excess tidal volume.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Every weight identifies a credible competing calculation; deleting the PBW removes the supported unique numerical order. Respiratory data establish why a protective order matters.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: If the checked PBW were 75 kg and plateau response permitted, 450 mL would be the initial target.

manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate, lower end: resident must reject a plausible dry-weight calculation, then prescribe an actual volume; arithmetic alone does not establish clinical approval.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: The independently checked PBW is 50 kg, while both scale measurements are higher. Counterfactual: If the checked PBW were 75 kg and plateau response permitted, 450 mL would be the initial target.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

originalProposedNodes.currentUpdate: Next hospital entry: tidal volume is now 300 mL with PBW 50 kg. During passive breaths, repeat plateau pressure is 32 cm H2O and measured total PEEP remains 10 cm H2O. Arterial pH is 7.36. The scale still reads 90 kg.

items.label: Acquisition
items.value: No inspiratory effort or leak during the repeated hold; airway secretions have been cleared.

choices.label: Reduce tidal volume to 250 mL
choices.rationale: Persistent plateau above 30 at 6 mL/kg supports a further step down to 5 mL/kg with reassessment.
choices.temptation: Apply the pressure constraint after the PBW target.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied matched measurements and pH.

choices.label: Maintain tidal volume at 300 mL
choices.rationale: A correct initial PBW calculation does not establish that persistent plateau elevation can be accepted while waiting for fluid loss.
choices.temptation: Treat six mL/kg as an endpoint that overrides pressure.
choices.correctUnder: Plateau at or below the protective goal with adequate gas exchange.

choices.label: Increase tidal volume to 350 mL
choices.rationale: Increasing delivered volume does not address the persisting distending-pressure problem.
choices.temptation: Use a volume within the broad 4–8 range without considering its pressure effect.
choices.correctUnder: A lower-pressure record with a separate supported need for more volume.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: At 6 mL/kg PBW, persistent plateau elevation still requires attention. The verified ARDSNet protocol steps volume down toward 5 and then 4 mL/kg while reassessing ventilation. For this record, 250 mL is the first smaller order. This new clinical meaning remains held for Melissa’s exact decision.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Recognize the current order already uses six mL/kg PBW and that plateau remains elevated under valid acquisition.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Apply the pressure constraint rather than repeat the weight-basis rule or wait for diuresis.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Wait for fluid removal because the initial six-mL/kg order appears correct.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Repeated passive plateau is 32 despite a current six-mL/kg prescription, with no severe acidemia supplied.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Unchanged scale indexing can conceal persistent overdistending pressure.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Removing plateau loses the reason to reduce below the initial target; removing current volume loses the fact that the initial target is already reached. The pH and acquisition protect the key boundary.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: If plateau were 27 at 300 mL with the same gas exchange, maintaining 300 mL would become reasonable.

answerChoices.label: Permeability edema with predicted-weight ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: The lung-injury course and low filling-pressure observation support permeability edema despite weight gain. In this ARDS context, tidal-volume selection uses predicted body weight rather than the scale measurement.

answerChoices.label: Hydrostatic edema with predicted-weight ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: The weight field is appropriate, but the mechanism does not fit the low measured filling pressure and acute aspiration/sepsis lung course as well as permeability injury.

answerChoices.label: Permeability edema with actual-weight ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: This recognizes the injury context and avoids the new fluid weight but still substitutes actual body weight for the anthropometric basis.

answerChoices.label: Hydrostatic edema with actual-weight ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: This assigns the pulmonary process from the weight gain and then uses a dry scale weight in place of the supported anthropometric basis.

decisionNodes.explanation: Positive fluid balance does not by itself classify the pulmonary process as hydrostatic edema. The aspiration/sepsis course, bilateral oxygenation problem and low measured filling pressure support the permeability-injury context. For an adult with ARDS, tidal-volume selection is based on predicted body weight from anthropometric measurements, not dry or fluid-loaded actual weight. No new numeric tidal-volume target, diagnostic ratio cutoff or calculation formula is taught.

originalProposedNodes.objective: Choose prone ventilation for persistent severe oxygenation impairment after protective optimization.
originalProposedNodes.currentUpdate: Later hospital entry: after volume and PEEP adjustment, plateau pressure is 28 cm H2O. PaO2 remains 58 mm Hg on FiO2 0.80 and PEEP 12 cm H2O. Blood pressure is stable. The spine is stable and the abdomen is closed.
originalProposedNodes.task: Which additional respiratory-support intervention best fits Nina Cole’s recorded condition?

choices.label: Begin prolonged prone ventilation
choices.rationale: Severe persistent oxygenation impairment after protective optimization supports proning before moving directly to extracorporeal support.
choices.temptation: Use both the oxygenation severity and completed optimization stage.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied persistent impairment without the stated contraindications.

choices.label: Continue supine protective ventilation
choices.rationale: Protective settings should continue, but the persistent severe oxygenation impairment supports adding prone positioning rather than retaining the same position.
choices.temptation: Treat improved plateau as sufficient recovery despite the oxygen requirement.
choices.correctUnder: Substantially improved oxygenation above the prone-eligibility range on otherwise appropriate support, or a contraindication requiring another plan.

choices.label: Begin venovenous ECMO cannulation
choices.rationale: ECMO is an important option for selected refractory cases; this record has not yet used the indicated prone strategy.
choices.temptation: Equate severe oxygenation impairment with exhaustion of conventional rescue.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent severe impairment after appropriate conventional rescue, assessed by an ECMO team.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: Interpret oxygenation together with support: 58/0.80 is approximately 73 mm Hg. Persistent impairment on adjusted protective ventilation favors prone positioning. An improved plateau does not establish oxygenation recovery. ECMO requires assessment of refractory disease after conventional strategies.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Infer persistent severe oxygenation impairment from PaO2 relative to FiO2 after optimization.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose the next supported rescue stage rather than equating an improved plateau with oxygenation recovery or moving prematurely to extracorporeal support.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Refer directly for ECMO because the oxygen tension remains low.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Severe impairment persists, but protective optimization has occurred and prone ventilation has not yet been used.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Remaining supine can omit a supported rescue strategy; immediate ECMO can bypass appropriate conventional rescue.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Deleting FiO2 removes severity interpretation; deleting completed optimization removes the escalation stage. Stable spine/closed abdomen define a clinical safety boundary.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: Repeated key-covered attack after repair: replaced a guideline-discouraged recruitment foil that had no credible correct-under setting with continued supine protection. Three concrete support plans now have real counterfactual indications. The normal plateau does not eliminate either rival without interpreting the oxygenation requirement.
manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: Three concrete respiratory-support plans at the same escalation point: prone protection, continued supine protection, or VV-ECMO cannulation. Shared protective care applies throughout.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer persistent severe oxygenation impairment from PaO2 relative to FiO2 after optimization. Then Choose the next supported rescue stage rather than equating an improved plateau with oxygenation recovery or moving prematurely to extracorporeal support.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard, predicted after repair: interpret severe hypoxemia under high oxygen support despite an acceptable plateau, then choose a rescue stage between ongoing conventional support and immediate ECMO.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: Severe impairment persists, but protective optimization has occurred and prone ventilation has not yet been used. Counterfactual: If oxygenation improved above the prone-eligibility range on the same protective settings, continued supine protection would become reasonable; persistent severe impairment after appropriate conventional rescue makes ECMO assessment more relevant.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

repairHistory.failedAttack: Prolonged high-pressure recruitment is discouraged without a credible setting where that exact distractor becomes best; this weakens its competing-plan value.
repairHistory.repair: Replaced with continued supine protective ventilation, whose appropriateness changes with the oxygenation response. Re-solved the support-stage comparison and repeated all five manual checks.

choices.label: Measure an end-inspiratory occlusion pressure
choices.rationale: Plateau measurement separates a dynamic peak-pressure rise from an increased static pressure burden before selecting an airway or lung intervention.
choices.temptation: Characterize mechanics before assuming the cause.
choices.correctUnder: Passive controlled ventilation with a new peak rise.

choices.label: Perform flexible bronchoscopic airway examination
choices.rationale: Bronchoscopy can evaluate selected persistent airway obstruction, but the peak signal has not yet distinguished a resistive from a static pressure problem.
choices.temptation: Assume mucus obstruction from an isolated dynamic maximum.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent suspected obstruction after simpler airway and pressure assessment.

choices.label: Perform thoracic pleural ultrasound examination
choices.rationale: Pleural assessment is valuable for a supported pneumothorax concern; peak pressure alone does not establish that target.
choices.temptation: Treat a high peak as a pleural distending-pressure event.
choices.correctUnder: A new static-pressure rise with compatible unilateral examination or instability.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: The peak is a dynamic maximum. An end-inspiratory pause during passive ventilation provides a static comparison that can direct the subsequent response. An unchanged delivered volume and stable oxygenation make a measured mechanics assessment appropriate in this record; this is not an instruction to delay emergency treatment in an unstable patient.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Recognize that an isolated peak rise does not establish resistance versus reduced compliance.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Select the pressure acquisition that distinguishes those mechanisms before a cause-specific intervention.

reasoning.decidingObservation: A matched passive pressure comparison is available from the current ventilator record; no static value has yet been acquired.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Assuming a cause can lead to unnecessary invasive airway testing or an incorrect volume change.

choices.label: Preoxygenate and suction the endotracheal tube
choices.rationale: The widening peak-to-plateau difference plus visible secretions supports airway clearance.
choices.temptation: Interpret the pressure pattern together with the airway observation.
choices.correctUnder: This supplied secretion-associated pattern.

choices.label: Administer an inhaled bronchodilator through the circuit
choices.rationale: Bronchospasm can increase resistance, but the supplied secretion findings favor suction as the first directed intervention.
choices.temptation: Treat every resistive rise as smooth-muscle narrowing.
choices.correctUnder: A compatible bronchospastic examination without visible retained secretions.

choices.label: Reduce the delivered tidal volume
choices.rationale: Volume reduction addresses excessive static pressure in selected records; unchanged plateau here points toward a different immediate target.
choices.temptation: React to peak pressure as if it were plateau pressure.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent excessive plateau at the current protective prescription.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: The static pressure is unchanged while the dynamic pressure difference widens. Visible secretions then identify a treatable airway contributor. Preoxygenated suction is appropriate; these measurements do not establish that all resistive loading is bronchospasm.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Interpret stable plateau with a larger dynamic gradient as a resistive change.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Use the airway finding to choose clearance rather than bronchodilation or reducing volume.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Choose a bronchodilator because resistance is high.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Visible tube secretions plus coarse sounds, with unchanged passive plateau.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: A missed airway obstruction can persist while a different setting is changed.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Delete the airway finding and bronchodilator becomes a credible rival; delete plateau and a static-pressure problem cannot be separated.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: If secretions were absent and new diffuse bronchospastic sounds dominated with the same mechanics, a bronchodilator would become reasonable.

originalProposedNodes.objective: Reduce breath frequency when incomplete exhalation causes intrinsic PEEP during severe obstructive ventilation.
originalProposedNodes.currentUpdate: Hospital record: during passive volume control for asthma, PaCO2 rises to 68 mm Hg and pH is 7.28. Blood pressure is stable. Bronchodilator therapy continues.

exhibit.caption: Independently constructed outside-hospital record; fictional measurements

originalProposedNodes.task: Which ventilator adjustment best fits Mark Price’s recorded pattern?

choices.label: Reduce the set respiratory rate
choices.rationale: More expiratory time addresses incomplete exhalation and intrinsic PEEP even though PaCO2 remains elevated.
choices.temptation: Prioritize the mechanics that caused trapping.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied persistent expiratory flow and total-PEEP excess.

choices.label: Increase the set respiratory rate
choices.rationale: Trying to normalize carbon dioxide by shortening expiration can worsen trapping.
choices.temptation: Treat the gas result without interpreting the expiratory record.
choices.correctUnder: Hypercapnia with complete exhalation and no intrinsic-PEEP concern, after reassessment.

choices.label: Increase the delivered tidal volume
choices.rationale: A larger breath can add trapped volume rather than resolve incomplete exhalation.
choices.temptation: Increase minute ventilation without accounting for expiratory limitation.
choices.correctUnder: A different low-volume record with complete expiration and acceptable distending pressure.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: The negative expiratory flow at the next inspiration and total PEEP above the set value indicate incomplete emptying. Reducing rate lengthens expiration. Follow gas exchange and pressures rather than trying to normalize PaCO2 by adding more frequent or larger breaths. No universal rate or acceptable-pH threshold is prescribed.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Infer incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP from flow and occlusion measurements.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose more expiratory time despite the temptation to increase minute ventilation for hypercapnia.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Increase rate to correct PaCO2.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Expiratory flow has not returned to zero and measured total PEEP exceeds set PEEP.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Increasing frequency can worsen trapped volume and intrathoracic pressure.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Removing the expiratory/PEEP observations makes increased rate a plausible hypercapnia response. The blood gas supplies the credible competing goal.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: If exhalation were complete, total PEEP equaled set PEEP and distending pressure allowed, a higher rate could become reasonable for hypercapnia.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No waveform diagnosis is supplied; a numeric sample table is used because the objective is interpreting recorded flow/occlusion values, not identifying an absent tracing. Three parallel adjustments; no rationale in labels.
manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: All offered choices are specific support or care plans at the recorded decision point. Rationales remain after answering.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP from flow and occlusion measurements. Then Choose more expiratory time despite the temptation to increase minute ventilation for hypercapnia.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard: a familiar response to hypercapnia is opposed by the actual expiratory mechanics. Rate action has one direct review with independent guideline support for assessing auto-PEEP.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: Expiratory flow has not returned to zero and measured total PEEP exceeds set PEEP. Counterfactual: If exhalation were complete, total PEEP equaled set PEEP and distending pressure allowed, a higher rate could become reasonable for hypercapnia.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

originalProposedNodes.sequenceReview: Standalone. No drug, sedation reversal, or acid-base calculation is scored.

originalProposedNodes.currentUpdate: Hospital record: during a monitored postoperative interval, oxygen consumption is unchanged on repeated indirect calorimetry. originalProposedNodes.task: Which assessment should have been prioritized to explain Brian Lewis’s recorded mixed-venous trend?

choices.label: Obtain transthoracic Doppler echocardiography
choices.rationale: Improved arterial carriage with unchanged consumption but lower mixed-venous saturation raises a blood-flow question; Doppler assessment can characterize cardiac output and function.
choices.temptation: Assess the remaining delivery component before attributing the trend to saturation or hemoglobin.
choices.correctUnder: This verified discordant record.

choices.label: Repeat the complete blood count
choices.rationale: The paired current blood counts show higher hemoglobin, so repeat measurement does not address the principal residual flow uncertainty.
choices.temptation: Treat low venous saturation as necessarily a hemoglobin-carriage problem.
choices.correctUnder: A new bleeding trajectory or uncertain/noncontemporaneous hemoglobin sample.

choices.label: Repeat the arterial blood gas
choices.rationale: Arterial oxygenation has improved in contemporaneous samples; repeating that measurement does not characterize the remaining flow component.
choices.temptation: Equate venous desaturation with persistent arterial oxygenation failure.
choices.correctUnder: An unreliable arterial sample or a new gas-exchange deterioration.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: The arterial measurements indicate improved oxygen carriage, while lower mixed-venous saturation at unchanged consumption indicates greater extraction. Assess flow rather than assuming normal saturation establishes adequate delivery. Doppler echocardiography can evaluate output and cardiac contributions; these observations do not diagnose a specific shock type or justify a particular fluid or inotrope order.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Integrate higher hemoglobin and arterial oxygenation with lower mixed-venous saturation at unchanged consumption.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Investigate the remaining blood-flow component rather than repeat the already contemporary carriage measurements.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Repeat arterial gas testing because the venous saturation fell.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Arterial carriage improves and consumption is unchanged while verified mixed-venous saturation falls.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Additional oxygen or hemoglobin-focused evaluation can miss a delivery problem in blood flow.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Deleting oxygen consumption reopens increased demand as an explanation; deleting arterial/hemoglobin data reopens those delivery components; removing provenance reopens sampling error.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: If the later arterial oxygenation had worsened or its sample provenance were uncertain, arterial gas reassessment would become appropriate.

decisionNodes.stem: Why can this patient's normal SpO2 coexist with reduced oxygen-carrying content?

answerChoices.label: Fewer hemoglobin carriers can have normal saturation
Normal saturation establishes a normal hemoglobin quantity
Reduced hemoglobin requires reduced oxygen saturation
The saturation percentage directly measures hemoglobin quantity

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Fewer hemoglobin carriers can have normal saturation.” Saturation describes how fully the available hemoglobin is occupied. Anemia reduces the available carrier quantity, so a normal fraction does not establish normal oxygen content.

originalProposedNodes.objective: Avoid delaying reintubation with rescue NIV for established post-extubation failure in a non-COPD medical patient.
originalProposedNodes.currentUpdate: Hospital record: after planned extubation for pneumonia, Elena develops increasing accessory-muscle use and fatigue. On high-flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.60, PaO2 is 54 mm Hg. PaCO2 rises from 39 to 59 mm Hg and pH falls to 7.26. She remains tired despite repositioning and airway clearance.
originalProposedNodes.task: Which respiratory-support plan best fits Elena Marsh’s recorded post-extubation deterioration?

choices.label: Reintubate and resume invasive ventilation
choices.rationale: The record now shows established worsening post-extubation respiratory failure in the population where rescue NIV may delay needed reintubation.
choices.temptation: Distinguish rescue after failure from prevention in a selected high-risk patient.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied fatigue and worsening gas exchange despite oxygen support.

choices.label: Begin rescue bilevel mask ventilation
choices.rationale: Preventive NIV evidence does not justify delaying reintubation for established failure in this non-COPD medical record.
choices.temptation: Transfer a successful preventive strategy to a later failure phase.
choices.correctUnder: Selected COPD hypercapnic failure or a separate evidence-supported postoperative context; not this medical population.

choices.label: Escalate high-flow nasal oxygen
choices.rationale: Further oxygen-focused support does not resolve the worsening ventilation and fatigue already present.
choices.temptation: Treat oxygen tension as the whole respiratory-support problem.
choices.correctUnder: An isolated oxygenation need with sustained ventilation and no progressive fatigue.

originalProposedNodes.explanation: This is rescue after deterioration, not prevention immediately after planned extubation. In general non-COPD medical patients with established post-extubation failure, ERS/ATS conditionally discourages NIV that may delay reintubation. The worsening ventilation and fatigue make continued oxygen escalation inadequate in this record. COPD and postoperative exceptions must not be erased.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Identify established respiratory failure after tube removal, including worsening ventilation rather than oxygenation alone.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose timely invasive support and avoid importing preventive NIV evidence into a different phase and population.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Use mask support because NIV is useful after some planned extubations.
reasoning.decidingObservation: This medical non-COPD patient is already deteriorating with fatigue and both oxygenation and ventilation impairment.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: A delayed reintubation can prolong unsupported failure.

originalProposedNodes.deletionTest: Delete chronology/population and the NIV evidence boundary changes; delete ventilation/fatigue and an oxygen-focused trial could be reasonable.
originalProposedNodes.counterfactual: In a suitable older COPD patient at the moment of planned extubation before failure develops, preventive bilevel support becomes reasonable.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All options are concrete support plans. Necessary no-COPD/nonoperative population details are retained for evidence scope, not as an unsupported universal contraindication.
manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: All offered choices are specific support or care plans at the recorded decision point. Rationales remain after answering.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Identify established respiratory failure after tube removal, including worsening ventilation rather than oxygenation alone. Then Choose timely invasive support and avoid importing preventive NIV evidence into a different phase and population.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard: distinguish prevention from rescue and separate population-specific exceptions while interpreting the current response. Conditional guidance is not portrayed as an absolute ban.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: This medical non-COPD patient is already deteriorating with fatigue and both oxygenation and ventilation impairment. Counterfactual: In a suitable older COPD patient at the moment of planned extubation before failure develops, preventive bilevel support becomes reasonable.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

originalProposedNodes.sequenceReview: Standalone so the COPD prevention explanation cannot directly rehearse this answer in the same encounter. Cross-case retrieval remains legitimate spaced learning.

originalQuestionDefinitions.stem: Which initial tidal-volume order best fits Nina Cole’s recorded lung-protective ventilation plan?

exhibit.caption: Independently constructed outside-hospital record; fictional measurements

answerChoices.label: Set tidal volume to 300 mL
answerChoices.rationale: Six times the checked 50-kg PBW gives 300 mL; the higher current prescription and plateau require protective reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Set tidal volume to 450 mL
answerChoices.rationale: This uses 6 mL/kg of the 75-kg pre-illness actual mass, which is not the lung-size basis.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses 6 mL/kg of the 75-kg pre-illness actual mass, which is not the lung-size basis.

answerChoices.label: Set tidal volume to 540 mL
answerChoices.rationale: This uses fluid-loaded actual mass and moves away from the protective prescription.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses fluid-loaded actual mass and moves away from the protective prescription.

originalQuestionDefinitions.explanation: Use the checked PBW for the initial 6-mL/kg order: 6 × 50 = 300 mL. Scale-weight changes do not enlarge the ventilated lung. The delivered volume and plateau must then be reassessed; this calculation does not guarantee the final setting.

originalQuestionDefinitions.stem: Which tidal-volume plan should have been chosen next for Nina Cole at this recorded assessment?

exhibit.caption: Independently constructed outside-hospital record; fictional observations

items.label: Acquisition
items.value: No inspiratory effort or leak during the repeated hold; airway secretions have been cleared.

items.label: Volume history
items.value: 300 mL is the current delivered volume, not a proposed future target.

answerChoices.label: Reduce tidal volume to 250 mL
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent plateau above 30 at 6 mL/kg supports a further step down to 5 mL/kg with reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Maintain tidal volume at 300 mL
answerChoices.rationale: A correct initial PBW calculation does not establish that persistent plateau elevation can be accepted while waiting for fluid loss.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A correct initial PBW calculation does not establish that persistent plateau elevation can be accepted while waiting for fluid loss.

answerChoices.label: Increase tidal volume to 350 mL
answerChoices.rationale: Increasing delivered volume does not address the persisting distending-pressure problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Increasing delivered volume does not address the persisting distending-pressure problem.

originalQuestionDefinitions.explanation: At 6 mL/kg PBW, persistent plateau elevation still requires attention. The verified ARDSNet protocol steps volume down toward 5 and then 4 mL/kg while reassessing ventilation. For this record, 250 mL is the first smaller order. This new clinical meaning remains held for Melissa’s exact decision.

answerChoices.label: Begin prolonged prone ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: Severe persistent oxygenation impairment after protective optimization supports proning before moving directly to extracorporeal support.

answerChoices.label: Continue supine protective ventilation
answerChoices.rationale: Protective settings should continue, but the persistent severe oxygenation impairment supports adding prone positioning rather than retaining the same position.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Protective settings should continue, but the persistent severe oxygenation impairment supports adding prone positioning rather than retaining the same position.

answerChoices.label: Begin venovenous ECMO cannulation
answerChoices.rationale: ECMO is an important option for selected refractory cases; this record has not yet used the indicated prone strategy.

originalQuestionDefinitions.explanation: Interpret oxygenation together with support: 58/0.80 is approximately 73 mm Hg. originalQuestionDefinitions.stem: Which assessment should first clarify Diane Foster’s peak-pressure rise at this recorded point?

answerChoices.label: Measure an end-inspiratory occlusion pressure
answerChoices.rationale: Plateau measurement separates a dynamic peak-pressure rise from an increased static pressure burden before selecting an airway or lung intervention.

answerChoices.label: Perform flexible bronchoscopic airway examination
answerChoices.rationale: Bronchoscopy can evaluate selected persistent airway obstruction, but the peak signal has not yet distinguished a resistive from a static pressure problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bronchoscopy can evaluate selected persistent airway obstruction, but the peak signal has not yet distinguished a resistive from a static pressure problem.

answerChoices.label: Perform thoracic pleural ultrasound examination
answerChoices.rationale: Pleural assessment is valuable for a supported pneumothorax concern; peak pressure alone does not establish that target.

decisionNodes.stem: Which assessment should first clarify Diane Foster’s peak-pressure rise at this recorded point?

answerChoices.label: Measure an end-inspiratory occlusion pressure
answerChoices.rationale: Plateau measurement separates a dynamic peak-pressure rise from an increased static pressure burden before selecting an airway or lung intervention.

answerChoices.label: Perform flexible bronchoscopic airway examination
answerChoices.rationale: Bronchoscopy can evaluate selected persistent airway obstruction, but the peak signal has not yet distinguished a resistive from a static pressure problem.

answerChoices.rationale: Pleural assessment is valuable for a supported pneumothorax concern; peak pressure alone does not establish that target.

decisionNodes.explanation: The peak is a dynamic maximum. An end-inspiratory pause during passive ventilation provides a static comparison that can direct the subsequent response. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Hospital record: Sarah follows commands and initiates breaths after pneumonia improves. PaO2 is 86 mm Hg on FiO2 0.35 and PEEP 5 cm H2O. Blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg without vasopressors. A brief unsupported sample reports an RSBI of 118 breaths/min/L.
decisionNodes.stem: Which liberation assessment should have been chosen next for Sarah Nguyen at this recorded point?

answerChoices.label: Perform a minimal-support spontaneous breathing trial
answerChoices.rationale: The global readiness observations support an SBT; a single RSBI need not be a mandatory gate.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the rapid shallow breathing index assessment
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the isolated index adds a gate rather than testing whether she tolerates an SBT.

answerChoices.label: Perform a stepwise SIMV rate-reduction trial
answerChoices.rationale: Gradually reducing mandatory rate can delay liberation when direct SBT readiness is present.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use recovery, spontaneous effort, oxygenation and circulatory stability to assess trial readiness. AARC does not require an RSBI calculation as a gate to an SBT. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Next hospital entry: a minimal-support breathing trial is charted as tolerated. Sarah remains comfortable, but its settings and measurements are recorded below.
decisionNodes.stem: Which plan best fits Sarah Nguyen’s recorded breathing trial before an extubation decision?

answerChoices.label: Repeat the trial at the preceding FiO2
answerChoices.rationale: The increased oxygen support can hide the oxygenation demand that the trial was meant to test.

answerChoices.label: Extubate to the trial oxygen concentration
answerChoices.rationale: The higher saturation occurred under greater oxygen support and does not by itself establish an equivalent trial.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the trial with added pressure support
answerChoices.rationale: Additional assistance changes another support input without resolving the oxygen-condition comparison.

decisionNodes.explanation: The saturation rose while FiO2 also rose. AARC conditionally favors retaining the preceding FiO2 during an SBT because increasing it may conceal an oxygenation limitation. authoringDefinition.objective: Reduce breath frequency when incomplete exhalation causes intrinsic PEEP during severe obstructive ventilation.
authoringDefinition.currentUpdate: Hospital record: during passive volume control for asthma, PaCO2 rises to 68 mm Hg and pH is 7.28. Blood pressure is stable. Bronchodilator therapy continues.

exhibit.caption: Independently constructed outside-hospital record; fictional measurements

authoringDefinition.task: Which ventilator adjustment best fits Mark Price’s recorded pattern?

choices.label: Reduce the set respiratory rate
choices.rationale: More expiratory time addresses incomplete exhalation and intrinsic PEEP even though PaCO2 remains elevated.
choices.temptation: Prioritize the mechanics that caused trapping.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied persistent expiratory flow and total-PEEP excess.

choices.label: Increase the set respiratory rate
choices.rationale: Trying to normalize carbon dioxide by shortening expiration can worsen trapping.
choices.temptation: Treat the gas result without interpreting the expiratory record.
choices.correctUnder: Hypercapnia with complete exhalation and no intrinsic-PEEP concern, after reassessment.

choices.label: Increase the delivered tidal volume
choices.rationale: A larger breath can add trapped volume rather than resolve incomplete exhalation.
choices.temptation: Increase minute ventilation without accounting for expiratory limitation.
choices.correctUnder: A different low-volume record with complete expiration and acceptable distending pressure.

authoringDefinition.explanation: The negative expiratory flow at the next inspiration and total PEEP above the set value indicate incomplete emptying. Reducing rate lengthens expiration. Follow gas exchange and pressures rather than trying to normalize PaCO2 by adding more frequent or larger breaths. No universal rate or acceptable-pH threshold is prescribed.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Infer incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP from flow and occlusion measurements.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose more expiratory time despite the temptation to increase minute ventilation for hypercapnia.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Increase rate to correct PaCO2.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Expiratory flow has not returned to zero and measured total PEEP exceeds set PEEP.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Increasing frequency can worsen trapped volume and intrathoracic pressure.

authoringDefinition.deletionTest: Removing the expiratory/PEEP observations makes increased rate a plausible hypercapnia response. The blood gas supplies the credible competing goal.
authoringDefinition.counterfactual: If exhalation were complete, total PEEP equaled set PEEP and distending pressure allowed, a higher rate could become reasonable for hypercapnia.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: No waveform diagnosis is supplied; a numeric sample table is used because the objective is interpreting recorded flow/occlusion values, not identifying an absent tracing. Three parallel adjustments; no rationale in labels.
manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: All offered choices are specific support or care plans at the recorded decision point. Rationales remain after answering.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Infer incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP from flow and occlusion measurements. Then Choose more expiratory time despite the temptation to increase minute ventilation for hypercapnia.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard: a familiar response to hypercapnia is opposed by the actual expiratory mechanics. Rate action has one direct review with independent guideline support for assessing auto-PEEP.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: Expiratory flow has not returned to zero and measured total PEEP exceeds set PEEP. Counterfactual: If exhalation were complete, total PEEP equaled set PEEP and distending pressure allowed, a higher rate could become reasonable for hypercapnia.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

authoringDefinition.sequenceReview: Standalone. No drug, sedation reversal, or acid-base calculation is scored.

choices.rationale: A suitable high-risk patient with chronic respiratory disease and hypercapnia can receive preventive NIV immediately after planned extubation.

choices.correctUnder: The tolerated trial with effective clearance in this older COPD patient.

choices.label: Extubate directly to standard nasal oxygen
choices.rationale: Standard oxygen offers less of the verified preventive ventilatory strategy for this selected high-risk hypercapnic profile.

choices.correctUnder: Persistent acute ventilatory deterioration or another unresolved extubation barrier.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Interpret residual hypercapnia against the documented baseline and the tolerated trial.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose preventive support at planned extubation rather than prolonged intubation for a reference-range target.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Continue invasive support until PaCO2 enters the laboratory interval.

reasoning.consequenceOfError: Waiting for an inapplicable gas target can prolong invasive support; omitting prevention may increase failure risk in selected high-risk patients.

authoringDefinition.deletionTest: Delete baseline and persistent acute acidosis becomes uncertain; delete airway-clearance data and planned extubation is not established. Chronic disease and age establish the preventive-support population.
authoringDefinition.counterfactual: Without chronic respiratory disease or other high-risk features after a valid trial, standard nasal oxygen becomes reasonable.

authoringDefinition.currentUpdate: Hospital record: after planned extubation for pneumonia, Elena develops increasing accessory-muscle use and fatigue. On high-flow nasal oxygen at FiO2 0.60, PaO2 is 54 mm Hg. PaCO2 rises from 39 to 59 mm Hg and pH falls to 7.26. She remains tired despite repositioning and airway clearance.
authoringDefinition.task: Which respiratory-support plan best fits Elena Marsh’s recorded post-extubation deterioration?

choices.label: Reintubate and resume invasive ventilation
choices.rationale: The record now shows established worsening post-extubation respiratory failure in the population where rescue NIV may delay needed reintubation.
choices.temptation: Distinguish rescue after failure from prevention in a selected high-risk patient.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied fatigue and worsening gas exchange despite oxygen support.

choices.label: Begin rescue bilevel mask ventilation
choices.rationale: Preventive NIV evidence does not justify delaying reintubation for established failure in this non-COPD medical record.
choices.temptation: Transfer a successful preventive strategy to a later failure phase.
choices.correctUnder: Selected COPD hypercapnic failure or a separate evidence-supported postoperative context; not this medical population.

choices.label: Escalate high-flow nasal oxygen
choices.rationale: Further oxygen-focused support does not resolve the worsening ventilation and fatigue already present.
choices.temptation: Treat oxygen tension as the whole respiratory-support problem.
choices.correctUnder: An isolated oxygenation need with sustained ventilation and no progressive fatigue.

authoringDefinition.explanation: This is rescue after deterioration, not prevention immediately after planned extubation. In general non-COPD medical patients with established post-extubation failure, ERS/ATS conditionally discourages NIV that may delay reintubation. The worsening ventilation and fatigue make continued oxygen escalation inadequate in this record. COPD and postoperative exceptions must not be erased.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Identify established respiratory failure after tube removal, including worsening ventilation rather than oxygenation alone.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose timely invasive support and avoid importing preventive NIV evidence into a different phase and population.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Use mask support because NIV is useful after some planned extubations.
reasoning.decidingObservation: This medical non-COPD patient is already deteriorating with fatigue and both oxygenation and ventilation impairment.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: A delayed reintubation can prolong unsupported failure.

authoringDefinition.deletionTest: Delete chronology/population and the NIV evidence boundary changes; delete ventilation/fatigue and an oxygen-focused trial could be reasonable.
authoringDefinition.counterfactual: In a suitable older COPD patient at the moment of planned extubation before failure develops, preventive bilevel support becomes reasonable.

manualAuthorGate.coverTheKey: All options are concrete support plans. Necessary no-COPD/nonoperative population details are retained for evidence scope, not as an unsupported universal contraindication.
manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: All offered choices are specific support or care plans at the recorded decision point. Rationales remain after answering.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Identify established respiratory failure after tube removal, including worsening ventilation rather than oxygenation alone. Then Choose timely invasive support and avoid importing preventive NIV evidence into a different phase and population.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Hard: distinguish prevention from rescue and separate population-specific exceptions while interpreting the current response. Conditional guidance is not portrayed as an absolute ban.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: This medical non-COPD patient is already deteriorating with fatigue and both oxygenation and ventilation impairment. Counterfactual: In a suitable older COPD patient at the moment of planned extubation before failure develops, preventive bilevel support becomes reasonable.
manualAuthorGate.residualConcern: Independent reviewer must challenge plausibility and difficulty; this is neither editorial PASS nor clinical approval.

authoringDefinition.sequenceReview: Standalone so the COPD prevention explanation cannot directly rehearse this answer in the same encounter. Cross-case retrieval remains legitimate spaced learning.

parkedAttempts.currentUpdate: Hospital record: the paired arterial and pulmonary-artery samples below were obtained at unchanged oxygen consumption. The pulmonary-artery catheter also produced concordant thermodilution runs showing a fall in flow during this interval. The record does not characterize ventricular function or preload responsiveness.

parkedAttempts.task: Which flow-assessment method should have been prioritized for Brian Lewis at this recorded point?

choices.label: Transthoracic Doppler echocardiography
choices.rationale: It can characterize cardiac function and flow, but the record does not establish it as uniquely prior to every other available assessment.
choices.temptation: Evaluate a cardiac contributor.
choices.correctUnder: Specific ventricular/function uncertainty that would change care.

choices.label: Passive leg raising with stroke-volume monitoring
choices.rationale: It can examine preload response; the supplied facts do not establish whether this or imaging should come first.
choices.temptation: Evaluate a preload contributor.
choices.correctUnder: A clinically supported preload-response question.

choices.label: Calibrated arterial waveform analysis
choices.rationale: It can contribute flow information, but already concordant thermodilution values do not establish why repeating flow with this method would outrank mechanism assessment.
choices.temptation: Verify flow with another technique.
choices.correctUnder: A clinically specified measurement or trending uncertainty.

parkedAttempts.explanation: Unkeyed and parked: the direction of the flow inference is supported, and the newly specified thermodilution availability removes the old context omission. Comparing three novel assessments removes the new-test-versus-redundant-repeat shortcut. The permitted source supports the methods, but does not uniquely rank their priority without a more specific clinical question.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Integrate higher hemoglobin and arterial oxygenation with lower mixed-venous saturation at unchanged consumption.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Investigate the remaining blood-flow component rather than repeat the already contemporary carriage measurements.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Repeat arterial gas testing because the venous saturation fell.
reasoning.decidingObservation: No sufficient deciding observation is supplied to choose among the equally novel methods.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: Additional oxygen or hemoglobin-focused evaluation can miss a delivery problem in blood flow.

parkedAttempts.deletionTest: Removing the numerical changes no longer leaves a novelty-based answer; no unique answer remains with them either. Uncertainty is preserved instead of assigning a key.
parkedAttempts.counterfactual: A specific ventricular/function uncertainty could favor Doppler echo, whereas a supported preload-responsiveness question could favor passive leg raising. Neither is established here.

manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: Three immediate hemodynamic assessments, each requiring its own clinical indication.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: A fall in flow is already measured; choosing the most useful next mechanism assessment still requires a patient-specific uncertainty that this record does not settle.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Indeterminate ranking, not hard difficulty. Parked with no key.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: Not established; three novel methods are not uniquely ranked by the available observations.

decisionNodes.stem: Why can this patient's normal SpO2 coexist with reduced oxygen-carrying content?

answerChoices.label: Fewer hemoglobin carriers can have normal saturation
Normal saturation establishes a normal hemoglobin quantity
Reduced hemoglobin requires reduced oxygen saturation
The saturation percentage directly measures hemoglobin quantity

decisionNodes.explanation: The correct answer is “Fewer hemoglobin carriers can have normal saturation.” Saturation describes how fully the available hemoglobin is occupied. Anemia reduces the available carrier quantity, so a normal fraction does not establish normal oxygen content.

revisedItems.objective: Choose prone ventilation for persistent severe oxygenation impairment after protective optimization.
revisedItems.currentUpdate: Later hospital entry: after volume and PEEP adjustment, plateau pressure is 28 cm H2O. PaO2 remains 58 mm Hg on FiO2 0.80 and PEEP 12 cm H2O. Blood pressure is stable. The spine is stable and the abdomen is closed.
revisedItems.task: Which respiratory-support plan should have been chosen next for Nina Cole at this recorded assessment?

choices.label: Begin prolonged prone ventilation
choices.rationale: Severe persistent oxygenation impairment after protective optimization supports proning before moving directly to extracorporeal support.
choices.temptation: Use both the oxygenation severity and completed optimization stage.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied persistent impairment without the stated contraindications.

choices.label: Continue supine protective ventilation
choices.rationale: Protective settings should continue, but the persistent severe oxygenation impairment supports adding prone positioning rather than retaining the same position.
choices.temptation: Treat improved plateau as sufficient recovery despite the oxygen requirement.
choices.correctUnder: Substantially improved oxygenation above the prone-eligibility range on otherwise appropriate support, or a contraindication requiring another plan.

choices.label: Begin venovenous ECMO cannulation
choices.rationale: ECMO is an important option for selected refractory cases; this record has not yet used the indicated prone strategy.
choices.temptation: Equate severe oxygenation impairment with exhaustion of conventional rescue.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent severe impairment after appropriate conventional rescue, assessed by an ECMO team.

revisedItems.explanation: Interpret oxygenation together with support: 58/0.80 is approximately 73 mm Hg. Persistent impairment on adjusted protective ventilation favors prone positioning. An improved plateau does not establish oxygenation recovery. ECMO requires assessment of refractory disease after conventional strategies.

reasoning.interpretFindings: Interpret persistent severe oxygenation impairment relative to the FiO2 after protective settings were adjusted.
reasoning.applyMeaning: Choose the next support stage between continued supine care, prone positioning and extracorporeal rescue.
reasoning.closestCredibleError: Continue supine care because plateau improved.
reasoning.decidingObservation: PaO2 remains 58 on FiO2 0.80 with PEEP 12 despite adjusted protective support.
reasoning.consequenceOfError: An acceptable plateau can coexist with a missed oxygenation rescue need.

revisedItems.deletionTest: Deleting FiO2 loses the oxygenation-severity inference; deleting completed optimization loses the rescue stage. Positioning-safety observations remain necessary and are not removed to hide the key.
revisedItems.counterfactual: If oxygenation improved above the prone-eligibility range at the same protective settings, continuing supine care would become reasonable; persistent refractory disease after conventional rescue supports ECMO assessment.

manualAuthorGate.sameStageAndCategory: Three named respiratory-support plans at the same escalation point; continued supine protection remains a real choice.
manualAuthorGate.twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret persistent severe oxygenation impairment relative to the FiO2 after protective settings were adjusted. Then Choose the next support stage between continued supine care, prone positioning and extracorporeal rescue.
manualAuthorGate.residentDifficulty: Moderate/hard: the existing clinically consequential chain is retained after eliminating the task shortcut.
manualAuthorGate.singleBestAnswer: PaO2 remains 58 on FiO2 0.80 with PEEP 12 despite adjusted protective support. Counterfactual: If oxygenation improved above the prone-eligibility range at the same protective settings, continuing supine care would become reasonable; persistent refractory disease after conventional rescue supports ECMO assessment.
